Luca Brasi is sent to investigate and is murdered. Gunmen then shoot Vito in the street. With the Don critically wounded, Sonny assumes command and prepares for war while Tom is briefly abducted and released with demands for a deal. Michael, still considered a civilian, finds his father's hospital room unguarded and realizes another attack is imminent. He moves Vito, recruits a frightened visitor to pose as protection, and faces Sollozzo's men until police arrive. Captain McCluskey, who is protecting Sollozzo, breaks Michael's jaw. The attack convinces Michael that legal status offers no safety and that he can no longer remain outside the conflict.

Sollozzo proposes a meeting with Michael, believing Vito's previously uninvolved son can negotiate peace. Michael instead volunteers to kill both Sollozzo and Captain McCluskey. Because killing a police officer will bring enormous pressure, the family verifies McCluskey's corruption and plans the act carefully. Clemenza teaches Michael how to use a hidden pistol and leave without hesitation. At an Italian restaurant, Michael retrieves the weapon from the lavatory and shoots both men. The family begins a public campaign exposing McCluskey's criminal ties while Michael is secretly sent to Sicily. His choice makes him a murderer and binds his future to the organization he had rejected. In New York, Sonny directs a violent struggle against the Tattaglias and their allies as Vito slowly recovers, but neither side can secure a clean victory.

The gang war settles into costly stalemate. Sonny's temper drives aggressive retaliation but also makes him predictable. Connie's marriage has become abusive; when Carlo beats her and she calls the Corleone home, Sonny races toward her without adequate protection. Gunmen ambush him at a toll plaza and kill him. Vito, recovered but grieving, resumes command and asks Bonasera to repair Sonny's body for burial, calling in the undertaker's wedding-day debt. Rather than continue a war that could endanger Michael, Vito summons the other Dons and agrees to peace and a limited accommodation with the narcotics trade. He promises not to avenge Sonny. Reading the meeting closely, he concludes that Barzini, not the more obvious Tattaglia, has directed the attack on his family. The peace is therefore a truce designed to bring Michael safely home, not an end to the struggle for control.

In Sicily, Michael lives under guard and learns more about the violence that shaped his father's generation. He falls in love with Apollonia Vitelli and marries her through local custom. Their brief marriage ends when a car bomb intended for Michael kills Apollonia, proving that the New York conflict reaches even his refuge. In New York, Vito's peace agreement stops the immediate war and permits the arrangements needed to bring Michael safely home. The losses of Sonny and Apollonia have nevertheless removed the futures the younger generation once expected. Barzini's hidden direction of the rival alliance remains unresolved, and Vito's promise not to seek vengeance limits what he can do openly. Michael returns with far less distance from his father's world than he possessed at Connie's wedding.

Back in the United States, Michael seeks out Kay, tells her he is now working with his father, and asks her to marry him while promising that the family will become legitimate. They begin a family, but Michael reveals only what supports that promised future. He visits Nevada and asserts control over the Corleones' plans there, rebuking Fredo for supporting casino operator Moe Greene against his own family. In New York, Clemenza and Tessio are told they must wait before forming independent organizations. Vito teaches Michael how rivals and trusted subordinates will test him, warning that Barzini will arrange a supposed peace meeting through a traitor close to the family. Vito then dies of a heart attack while playing with his grandson in the garden. At the funeral, Tessio offers to arrange the meeting with Barzini, confirming the warning. Rivals interpret Vito's death as their opportunity, while Michael maintains a calm appearance and completes the plans his father helped him design.

Michael stands as godfather at the baptism of Connie and Carlo's child while his organization executes a coordinated attack. Barzini, Tattaglia, and other enemy leaders are killed, as is Moe Greene, removing opposition in both New York and Nevada. Tessio's attempt to deliver Michael to Barzini is exposed; he asks Tom to save him but is taken away for execution. Michael then confronts Carlo. After obtaining his confession that he helped set Sonny's fatal ambush, Michael has Clemenza strangle him despite promising that he would merely be expelled from the family. Connie accuses Michael of killing her husband. He denies the charge to Kay, but she eventually learns from Tom enough to recognize the truth and the position Michael now occupies. She leaves, then returns with their children and adopts Catholic prayer as a way to hope for his soul. As the family prepares to relocate to Nevada, Michael is firmly established as Don: he has preserved the Corleone empire by becoming the calculating criminal ruler he once promised Kay he would never be.

characters.description: The Virginia-born fighting man who has spent ten years on Earth after being separated from Barsoom, his wife Dejah Thoris, and their unborn child. When he is transported back, he arrives in the Valley Dor rather than Helium and immediately has to survive its hostile inhabitants.
characters.name: John Carter

characters.description: Jeddak of the Tharks and Carter's close friend from his earlier life on Barsoom. Carter finds him fighting for survival in the Valley Dor, where Tars had arrived after following the pilgrimage that Barsoomian religion presents as a final journey.
characters.name: Tars Tarkas

characters.description: A red Martian princess held in the domain of the therns. Thuvia understands the dangerous creatures of the Valley Dor and can control banths through learned commands, making her an important guide and ally during the escape.
characters.name: Thuvia

characters.description: A high-ranking warrior of the First Born, the black Martian people whose raiders dominate the hidden Sea of Omean. Xodar meets Carter as an enemy and is confident in the First Born's superiority and in the divine status of their ruler, Issus.
characters.name: Xodar

characters.description: A daughter of Matai Shang and a princess among the white-skinned therns. Phaidor has been raised to regard the therns as a sacred ruling order. Her attraction to Carter and her possessiveness toward him place her in an uneasy relationship with the other captives.
characters.name: Phaidor

characters.description: The highest-ranking leader of the therns and Phaidor's father. Matai Shang benefits from the religious system surrounding the Valley Dor and treats exposure of its workings as a threat to his order's authority.
characters.name: Matai Shang

characters.description: The ruler worshiped by the First Born as the source of Barsoomian life and death. Issus presides over a hidden court beneath the Valley Dor, uses ritual and fear to preserve her position, and regards prisoners as disposable entertainment.
characters.name: Issus

characters.description: Carter's wife and the princess of Helium, from whom he has been separated for ten Earth years. When he finally sees her again, she is a prisoner in Issus's domain and does not yet know that he has returned to Barsoom.
characters.name: Dejah Thoris

characters.description: A Heliumite officer and Carter's trusted ally. Kantos Kan remains loyal when Carter returns from the forbidden Valley Dor and helps him despite the religious and political charges attached to that return.
characters.name: Kantos Kan

characters.description: The jed of Zodanga who holds power in Helium while Tardos Mors and Mors Kajak are absent. Zat Arras treats Carter's return from the Valley Dor as both heresy and a challenge to his own authority and orders him confined.
characters.name: Zat Arras

characters.description: The grown son of John Carter and Dejah Thoris, born after Carter's disappearance. Carthoris is a prince and military leader of Helium who recognizes his father from family accounts and supports his effort to recover Dejah.
characters.name: Carthoris

characters.description: The jeddak of Helium and Dejah Thoris's grandfather. Tardos Mors remains one of Carter's principal political allies and supports the attempt to rescue the captives after returning to Helium.
characters.name: Tardos Mors

recaps.ending: Carter's coalition attacks the domains of the therns and First Born. Issus is exposed as mortal and loses the obedience on which her rule depends; her regime collapses, while Xodar rises among the freed First Born. Dejah, Thuvia, and Phaidor are sealed inside the Temple of the Sun, whose chambers open to the outside only once during a Barsoomian year. Carter can do nothing but watch the rotating prison from outside. As the doorway carrying the women passes from sight, he sees Phaidor raising a knife toward Dejah. The opening closes before he can intervene, leaving Dejah and Thuvia trapped and Dejah in immediate danger from Phaidor.
recaps.in_short: After ten years on Earth, John Carter returns to Barsoom in the Valley Dor, where he reunites with Tars Tarkas and learns that the planet's promised pilgrimage ends in predation and captivity. They rescue Thuvia of Ptarth, confront the white therns who maintain the religious deception, and are drawn into the hidden realm of the First Born beneath the valley. Carter meets the warrior Xodar and exposes the supposedly divine Issus as a mortal ruler. He also finds Dejah Thoris alive but imprisoned. After escaping, Carter returns to Helium, meets his grown son Carthoris, survives prosecution for returning from the Valley Dor, and gathers an alliance to free the captives. The attack destroys Issus's authority, but Matai Shang seals Dejah, Thuvia, and Phaidor inside the rotating Temple of the Sun for a full Barsoomian year. As their chamber closes, Carter sees the jealous Phaidor raise a knife against Dejah and cannot reach her.

recaps.text: Previously: John Carter was transported from an Arizona cave to Barsoom, where the planet's lower gravity gave him unusual strength. Captured by green Martians, he befriended Tars Tarkas, Sola, and Woola, and fell in love with Dejah Thoris, princess of Helium. He united Thark warriors with Helium, stopped Dejah's forced marriage to the prince of Zodanga, and helped defeat that city. Tars Tarkas became jeddak of the Tharks, while Carter married Dejah. Nine years later, with Dejah expecting their child, the atmosphere plant sustaining Barsoom failed. Carter entered the sealed facility and restarted its machinery, but immediately woke in his body on Earth. Ten years passed there without any sign from Barsoom, so he did not know whether the planet, Dejah, or their child had survived.

Carter is finally transported back to Barsoom but arrives in the Valley Dor, the destination of the voluntary pilgrimage that Barsoomians are taught to regard as sacred and final. The valley is instead filled with plant men and great white apes that attack new arrivals. Carter unexpectedly finds Tars Tarkas and fights beside him. In the surrounding caverns they learn that white-skinned therns exploit the pilgrims and preserve the religion that sends victims into the valley. They meet Thuvia, a captive princess of Ptarth who understands the valley's creatures and can command its banths. The three seek a path out while the therns try to prevent them from carrying what they have learned back to the wider world.

Carter, Tars Tarkas, and Thuvia escape the immediate dangers of the Valley Dor but enter the conflict between the therns and the First Born, black Martian raiders who travel through the hidden Sea of Omean. Carter fights Xodar, a senior First Born warrior, and is carried into the underground realm ruled by Issus. Phaidor, daughter of the thern leader Matai Shang, is among the prisoners drawn into the same struggle. Her religious certainty and interest in Carter make her a volatile companion. The layers of authority are now clearer: ordinary Barsoomians revere a pilgrimage controlled by the therns, while the therns themselves fear the First Born, who in turn worship Issus.

In Issus's court, Carter discovers that the supposed goddess is a mortal ruler who maintains power through secrecy, ritual, and the unquestioning loyalty of the First Born. He sees Dejah alive among the captives, along with Thuvia and Phaidor, but cannot free them immediately. Issus sends Carter and Xodar to the prison island of Shador. When Xodar learns that his ruler is willing to discard even faithful servants, his certainty in her divinity breaks, and he joins Carter. They organize an escape and begin turning the First Born's own routes and machines against Issus's regime. Carter's purpose is now both personal and political: reach Dejah and expose the linked systems that have kept the Valley Dor and Omean beyond challenge.

Carter and Xodar escape the First Born and eventually reach Helium, where Carter expects help. Instead, his return from the Valley Dor violates a deeply rooted religious prohibition, and Zat Arras, the Zodangan jed exercising authority in the city, orders him arrested. Carter is reunited with loyal allies including Kantos Kan but finds that Dejah remains a prisoner and that public belief makes an open rescue difficult. He also learns that the child Dejah was expecting when he vanished survived: Carthoris is now a grown prince of Helium. Father and son meet for the first time while Carter faces judgment for bringing forbidden knowledge back from the pilgrimage.

Carter is condemned under the old religious law, but Carthoris, Kantos Kan, and other loyalists help him escape. Evidence of the deception in the Valley Dor begins to weaken the authority behind the sentence. With support from Helium, Ptarth, the Tharks, and Xodar's allies, Carter gathers a fleet for a direct assault on the therns and the First Born. Zat Arras attempts to obstruct and then exploit the expedition, but Carter retains the loyalty of the forces committed to freeing the prisoners. The coalition reaches the hidden domains around Omean and begins the battle to overthrow Issus's court and recover Dejah, Thuvia, and Phaidor.

Carter's allied forces break into the hidden strongholds. Issus is publicly exposed as mortal, and the First Born turn against the ruler they had worshiped; her regime collapses, and Xodar emerges as a leader among his people. Dejah, Thuvia, and Phaidor are sealed in one of the rotating chambers of the Temple of the Sun, each of which opens to the outside only once in a Barsoomian year. Carter remains beside the temple, unable to force an entrance. In the final instant before the chamber moves fully out of view, he sees Phaidor raise a knife toward Dejah. The door closes, leaving Thuvia and Dejah trapped and Dejah facing an immediate attack while Carter can only wait outside.

characters.description: An educated young traveler whose fascination with magic takes him to Thessaly. Curious, impulsive, and strongly drawn to sensual adventure, he listens eagerly to tales of witchcraft and looks for a chance to witness it himself.
characters.name: Lucius

characters.description: A traveler Lucius meets on the road to Hypata. He recounts a disturbing story about his friend Socrates and the witch Meroe, giving Lucius his first extended example of the supernatural dangers associated with Thessaly.
characters.name: Aristomenes

characters.description: A miserly but prosperous citizen of Hypata who hosts Lucius through a family connection. His household offers little comfort, but his marriage to Pamphile places Lucius close to the magic he is eager to investigate.
characters.name: Milo

characters.description: Milo's wife, widely reputed in Hypata to be a powerful witch. Lucius is warned that she uses magic in pursuit of men who attract her and punishes anyone who obstructs her desires.
characters.name: Pamphile

characters.description: A servant in Milo's household who becomes Lucius's lover. Playful and resourceful, she has access to Pamphile's private rooms and reluctantly agrees to help Lucius observe her mistress's magic.
characters.name: Fotis

characters.description: A wealthy woman in Hypata who recognizes Lucius as a relative through his mother's family. She welcomes him generously and warns him that Pamphile's apparent respectability conceals dangerous magical practices.
characters.name: Byrrhena

characters.description: A young woman abducted by robbers shortly before her wedding. Held in their cave and terrified for her future, she is comforted by an old attendant who tells her the story of Cupid and Psyche.
characters.name: Charite

characters.description: A princess in the old woman's tale whose extraordinary beauty brings worship from strangers but leaves her without a husband. An oracle sends her to a mysterious marriage, beginning a long test of trust, endurance, and divine hostility.
characters.name: Psyche

characters.description: The goddess of love in the tale of Psyche. Angered that a mortal woman's beauty is drawing away her honors, she orders her son Cupid to arrange a degrading match for the unsuspecting princess.
characters.name: Venus

characters.description: Venus's son, whom she orders to make Psyche fall in love with a degrading match. He disappears from the old woman's account just as Psyche is carried to a palace and visited by a mysterious husband who will not let her see him.
characters.name: Cupid

characters.description: Charite's fiancé, from whom she was abducted shortly before their wedding. Her hope that he is still searching for her gives the captive a personal future beyond the robbers' cave.
characters.name: Tlepolemus

characters.description: A supposed friend of Tlepolemus who is consumed by desire for Charite. After ordinary courtship proves impossible, his concealed obsession makes him a grave danger to the married couple.
characters.name: Thrasyllus

characters.description: A wandering group of fraudulent devotees who buy Lucius and use public performances, fortune-telling, and displays of religious excitement to obtain money and food. Their private conduct repeatedly exposes the gap between their sacred claims and their behavior.
characters.name: The Wandering Priests

characters.description: A wealthy Corinthian who acquires Lucius after learning that the ass enjoys human food and can perform trained tricks. He plans to make the remarkable animal part of an elaborate public entertainment.
characters.name: Thiasus

characters.description: The goddess who answers Lucius when he prays beside the sea in utter desperation. She appears as a universal divine protector and promises release if he approaches her festival procession and accepts a life of grateful service afterward.
characters.name: Isis

recaps.ending: Having fled the Corinthian spectacle, Lucius reaches the shore at Cenchreae and prays for divine aid. Isis appears in a dream and directs him to her festival. During the procession he eats roses carried by a priest and immediately regains his human body. The priest explains that Lucius's reckless appetites caused his misery and that freedom now carries an obligation to the goddess. Lucius joins her worship, submits to initiation after waiting for the proper sign, and later travels to Rome. There he undergoes further initiations connected with Isis and Osiris, despite the expense and his occasional uncertainty about why more rites are required. He supports himself as an advocate and receives a place among the cult's officials. The narrative closes with Lucius willingly shaving his head and publicly serving the religion that delivered him, replacing his earlier restless curiosity with disciplined devotion.
recaps.in_short: Lucius travels through Thessaly in search of magic and persuades the servant Fotis to let him try a witch's ointment. A mistake transforms him into an ass, though he keeps his human mind and can be restored by eating roses. Before he can do so, robbers seize him, beginning a long passage through violent and exploitative owners. In the robbers' cave he hears the tale of Cupid and Psyche, whose suffering ends in divine marriage and immortality, and he briefly helps the captive Charite. Her rescue and marriage give way to tragedy when Thrasyllus murders her husband and she kills herself after taking revenge. Lucius then passes among fraudulent priests, mill workers, soldiers, cooks, and entertainers, observing adultery, cruelty, greed, and sudden reversals of fortune. Faced with forced participation in a public sexual spectacle at Corinth, he escapes to the coast. Isis answers his prayer, provides roses that restore his human form, and draws him into a lasting religious vocation culminating in initiation and priestly service at Rome.

recaps.text: Lucius travels toward Hypata in Thessaly, a region famous for magic. On the road he meets Aristomenes, who tells how his missing friend Socrates was impoverished and living in fear after becoming involved with the witch Meroe. Aristomenes tried to help him leave, but Meroe and another woman entered their locked room by supernatural means, attacked Socrates, and magically concealed his wound. He died when the enchantment failed during the next stage of their journey. Lucius's companion dismisses the account, but it increases Lucius's curiosity. In Hypata, Lucius stays with Milo, a wealthy and extremely frugal acquaintance connected to his mother's family. Milo's household looks ordinary, yet the stories Lucius has heard encourage him to treat every unusual event as possible evidence of enchantment. His desire to experience magic directly, rather than avoid its dangers, is already guiding his choices.

Lucius's wealthy relative Byrrhena welcomes him and warns that Milo's wife Pamphile is a dangerous witch. Instead of withdrawing, Lucius begins an affair with Pamphile's servant Fotis so that he can get closer to her mistress's secrets. At Byrrhena's dinner he hears another grim account of witchcraft, then returns home and attacks three shapes he believes are armed intruders. The next day he is put on public trial, only to discover that the proceeding is part of Hypata's Festival of Laughter and that his victims were enchanted wineskins. Fotis admits her role in the trick and later lets him watch Pamphile use an ointment to become an owl. Lucius asks to imitate her, but Fotis gives him the wrong jar and he becomes an ass while retaining human awareness. Roses would reverse the change, yet robbers raid Milo's house before he can eat any and carry him away with their loot.

Still trapped as an ass, Lucius is driven hard by Milo's robbers and repeatedly misses chances to reach roses. At their mountain hideout he hears the men recount raids in which several companions died. The band then brings in Charite, a young woman abducted shortly before her wedding to Tlepolemus. When a dream leaves her terrified, the old woman guarding the cave begins the story of Cupid and Psyche. Psyche is a mortal princess whose beauty attracts worship that Venus believes belongs to her. Venus orders Cupid to punish her, while an oracle directs Psyche's family to abandon her for a monstrous bridegroom. Instead, she is carried to a marvelous palace where invisible servants provide every comfort, and she is visited at night by a husband she is forbidden to see. Her jealous sisters persuade her that the unknown husband must be a monster and urge her to uncover his identity.

Psyche lights a lamp over her sleeping husband and discovers that he is Cupid. Startled, she wounds him with hot oil, and he leaves because she broke their agreement. After the sisters who misled her die through their own ambition, Psyche searches for Cupid and finally surrenders to Venus. The goddess beats and humiliates her, then imposes a series of impossible tasks, but ants, a reed, an eagle, and other helpers enable Psyche to complete them. Her last journey takes her to the underworld for a portion of Proserpina's beauty. She opens the container and falls into a deathlike sleep; Cupid revives her, appeals to Jupiter, and obtains a lasting settlement. Jupiter makes Psyche immortal, the marriage is formally accepted, and their child is born. Back in the robbers' cave, Lucius tries to escape with Charite. They are recaptured, and the robbers plan a brutal joint punishment for them, leaving both in immediate danger.

Tlepolemus, Charite's fiancé, enters the robbers' cave disguised as a famous outlaw called Haemus. He wins the band's confidence, drugs them with wine, frees Charite, and arranges the robbers' capture and death. Lucius expects a reward but instead remains livestock and suffers under careless or sadistic handlers on the couple's estate. His fortunes worsen again after a vicious boy who tormented him is killed by a bear and the boy's mother demands the ass's death. The narrative then turns to Charite's household. Thrasyllus, secretly obsessed with her, murders Tlepolemus during a hunt and pretends the death was accidental. Tlepolemus's ghost reveals the truth to Charite. She feigns acceptance of Thrasyllus, blinds him with a hairpin while he sleeps, and kills herself at her husband's tomb. Thrasyllus shuts himself inside the tomb to die. Lucius is sold and falls into the hands of wandering priests whose fraudulent performances and predatory behavior bring fresh danger.

Lucius continues to pass between owners and witnesses a broad range of domestic cruelty, sexual deception, poverty, and abuse. At a mill he observes the harsh treatment of workers and animals and the miller's wife's affair; after her plot is exposed, supernatural vengeance leads to the miller's death. Lucius later belongs to a gardener and then a soldier before entering the household of two brothers, one a cook and one a pastry maker. They discover that the ass secretly eats prepared human food. Their wealthy master Thiasus is delighted, teaches Lucius to dine and perform tricks, and takes him to Corinth as a public curiosity. A condemned woman is selected to have sex with him during an arena spectacle before she is killed by beasts. Lucius, unwilling to be part of the exhibition and afraid that the animals may attack him too, escapes while his keepers are occupied and runs to the nearby coast at Cenchreae.

Alone beside the sea, Lucius prays for rescue. Isis appears to him in a dream, identifies herself as a universal goddess, and tells him to attend her approaching festival. In the procession, a priest carries the roses she promised; Lucius eats them and returns to human form before the crowd. The priest interprets his years as an ass as the result of reckless curiosity and appetite, and Lucius accepts the obligation to devote his restored life to Isis. After a period of preparation and uncertainty over the cost, he receives a divine sign and undergoes a secret initiation. He later travels to Rome, where further instructions lead him through additional rites associated with Isis and Osiris. Lucius earns a living in the courts and is admitted to a religious office. He ends the account not by returning to his former pleasures but by embracing a visible, disciplined life of priestly service, grateful for the deliverance that ended his animal wandering.

characters.description: A prosperous, educated young man traveling through Thessaly, a region associated with magic. Intensely curious about supernatural practices and confident that he can approach them without lasting harm, he narrates both his own adventures and the many stories he hears along the way.
characters.name: Lucius

characters.description: A fellow traveler Lucius meets on the road to Hypata. Ridiculed by another traveler, he tells Lucius about his disastrous involvement with his friend Socrates and the feared witch Meroe, establishing the dangers of the magic Lucius is eager to investigate.
characters.name: Aristomenes

characters.description: Lucius's host in Hypata, a wealthy moneylender notorious for living as though he were poor. Suspicious and miserly, he offers minimal hospitality while leaving Lucius close to the magical household he wants to observe.
characters.name: Milo

characters.description: Milo's wife, widely feared as a powerful witch who pursues young men and punishes those who resist or disappoint her. Lucius's desire to witness her transformations draws him deeper into the household's secrets.
characters.name: Pamphile

characters.description: A servant in Milo and Pamphile's household who becomes Lucius's lover. Lively and resourceful, she gives him access to Pamphile's hidden magical practices, though she is less exact in handling them than Lucius assumes.
characters.name: Fotis

characters.description: A wealthy relative of Lucius in Hypata who welcomes him lavishly and warns him that Pamphile is a dangerous witch. Her household hosts the dinner at which Thelyphron recounts his grotesque experience guarding a corpse.
characters.name: Byrrhena

characters.description: A young woman abducted by the bandits who also steal Lucius in his transformed state. Grieving and terrified after being taken shortly before her wedding, she listens while the bandits' old housekeeper tries to console her with the story of Cupid and Psyche.
characters.name: Charite

characters.description: The youngest of three royal daughters in a story told to Charite. Her extraordinary beauty brings worship from strangers but isolates her from ordinary marriage and provokes Venus's anger. An oracle orders her family to leave her exposed for a mysterious bridegroom.
characters.name: Psyche

characters.description: The goddess of love and beauty, offended when mortals transfer their admiration from her to Psyche. She orders her son to make the princess fall in love with a degraded husband as punishment for receiving honors meant for a goddess.
characters.name: Venus

characters.description: Venus's son and Psyche's unseen husband. He visits Psyche only in darkness and forbids her to look at him, trying to keep their marriage hidden from his mother. His identity becomes clear when Psyche examines him by lamplight.
characters.name: Cupid

characters.description: Charite's fiancé, from whom she was taken shortly before their wedding. Her memories of him deepen her grief in captivity and make reunion with him the hope behind her attempts to escape.
characters.name: Tlepolemus

characters.description: A supposed friend of Tlepolemus whose desire for Charite makes him treacherous. After engineering Tlepolemus's death, he approaches the grieving widow with a false account and an offer of marriage.
characters.name: Thrasyllus

characters.description: A group of wandering devotees who buy Lucius and use him to carry their image and supplies while they solicit gifts through ecstatic performances. Their hidden conduct repeatedly puts both their livelihood and Lucius at risk.
characters.name: Priests of the Syrian Goddess

characters.description: The goddess who answers Lucius when he reaches the seashore in despair. Appearing in a dream under a universal divine identity, she promises release if he trusts her procession and thereafter asks for his disciplined religious service.
characters.name: Isis

recaps.ending: At Cenchreae, Lucius prays beside the sea and sees the goddess Isis in a dream. She tells him to approach her public procession and eat the roses carried by a priest. He obeys, sheds the ass's body, and becomes human again before the crowd. The priest explains that Lucius's reckless curiosity subjected him to Fortune, while Isis has now claimed him for a more ordered life. Lucius joins her worship, undergoes a costly and secret initiation, and later travels to Rome. Further dreams direct him toward additional initiations, including the mysteries associated with Osiris. Though anxious about the expense and repeated commands, he accepts them as divine guidance. The narrative ends with Lucius admitted to religious service in Rome, his head shaved as a public sign of office. His physical metamorphosis has been reversed, but his experiences have permanently changed his allegiance and way of life.
recaps.in_short: Lucius travels in Thessaly seeking magic and, with help from the servant Fotis, secretly watches her mistress become an owl. He tries the ointment himself but is accidentally changed into an ass; roses can restore him, yet repeated mishaps keep them out of reach. Stolen by bandits, abused by successive owners, and exposed to stories of violence, desire, and deception, he witnesses human society from the position of an animal. Among the embedded tales is that of Psyche, whose forbidden sight of Cupid separates them until she completes Venus's ordeals and is made immortal. Lucius repeatedly approaches rescue but passes instead through bandits, priests, a mill, farms, and wealthy households. When he is to be displayed in a degrading public spectacle, he escapes to the shore. Isis answers his prayer and directs him to roses in her procession. Restored to human form, Lucius devotes himself to her worship, undergoes initiation, and ends as a religious servant in Rome.

recaps.text: Lucius travels through Thessaly, eager to investigate the magic for which the region is famous. On the road he meets Aristomenes, who tells how his friend Socrates fell under the power of the witch Meroe and died despite their attempt to escape her. Rather than discouraging Lucius, the story strengthens his curiosity. In Hypata he stays with Milo, a rich but miserly moneylender connected to Lucius's family. Milo's household offers little comfort, but it places Lucius in the city where he hopes to encounter supernatural practices. The opening establishes a pattern in which travelers and hosts exchange extraordinary stories while Lucius treats warnings as invitations to seek the same dangers for himself.

In Hypata, Lucius's relative Byrrhena warns him that Milo's wife Pamphile is a powerful witch. Lucius begins an affair with the servant Fotis precisely because she can give him access to Pamphile's secrets. After a night in which he believes he has killed three attackers, he is publicly tried, only to learn that the proceedings are the city's Festival of Laughter and that his victims were enchanted wineskins. Fotis admits her part in the magic and later lets him watch Pamphile use an ointment to become an owl. Lucius demands to try it, but Fotis gives him the wrong container and he becomes an ass while retaining his human mind. He can be restored by eating roses, yet before he can reach any, robbers raid Milo's house, load their loot onto him, and drive him away with their animals.

As a pack animal for the bandits, Lucius suffers beatings, hunger, dangerous roads, and repeated failures to reach roses. The robbers bring a young captive named Charite to their cave. Their old housekeeper tries to comfort her by telling the story of Psyche, a princess whose beauty provokes the anger of Venus. Psyche is abandoned in accordance with an oracle but carried to a marvelous palace, where an unseen husband visits her at night and forbids her to look at him. Her jealous sisters persuade her that he must be a monster. Psyche lights a lamp while he sleeps and discovers Cupid, but hot oil wakes him and he leaves because she broke his trust. Her sisters die through their own schemes, and Psyche begins searching for her husband while Venus prepares to punish her. Lucius remains captive as the inset story continues.

Psyche submits to Venus, who assigns a series of seemingly impossible tasks. With supernatural help she sorts mixed seeds, gathers dangerous golden wool, collects water from a sheer height, and descends to the underworld for a portion of Proserpina's beauty. Curiosity again causes disaster when she opens the container and falls into a deathlike sleep, but Cupid revives her and appeals to Jupiter. Psyche is made immortal, her marriage to Cupid is recognized, and Venus accepts the settlement. Back in the main narrative, Lucius and Charite attempt to escape but are recaptured. Charite's fiancé Tlepolemus then enters the bandit company disguised as the outlaw Haemus, drugs the robbers, and rescues both Charite and Lucius. Lucius is honored for helping her, but life as an ass remains precarious, and cruelty from those tending the animals soon places him in danger again.

Charite's apparent rescue ends tragically when Thrasyllus, who desires her, arranges Tlepolemus's death during a hunt. Tlepolemus's ghost reveals the truth in a dream. Charite blinds Thrasyllus and kills herself at her husband's tomb; Thrasyllus then seals himself inside the tomb to die. Lucius is sold to wandering priests of the Syrian Goddess and carries their sacred objects while witnessing the deception and sexual secrecy behind their performances. After their arrest, he passes through more owners, including a miller. At the mill he sees exhausting human and animal labor, as well as the schemes surrounding the miller's unfaithful wife. Her revenge, aided by a woman practicing magic, brings about the miller's death. Lucius is sold again, moving from a gardener's poor but relatively gentle household into further conflict when a soldier claims him by force.

Lucius eventually belongs to two brothers, a cook and a pastry maker, whose master discovers that the ass secretly eats elaborate human food. Lucius becomes a profitable curiosity, demonstrating trained behavior to guests. Plans are made to exhibit him in the arena with a condemned woman, but he understands the humiliation and danger and escapes to the coast at Cenchreae. There he prays to the divine power of the moon. Isis appears in a dream and tells him to join her procession and eat roses from a priest's garland. The next day he follows her instructions and is restored publicly to human form. Lucius commits himself to Isis, undergoes initiation into her mysteries, and travels to Rome. Further divine instructions lead to additional initiations and service associated with Osiris. He ends not by returning to his earlier carefree life, but as a devoted religious official whose transformed understanding gives his wanderings a final order.
